🚦 Introduction: what a rate limiter is and why we need one

Hinglish samajh: Rate limiter ek aisa component hai jo tay karta hai ki koi client ek time window mein kitni requests bhej sakta hai. Limit paar hone par extra requests rok di jaati hain. Iske teen fayde hain: DoS attack se bachav, kharcha kam karna (khaaskar paid third-party API mein), aur overload se bachana. Is chapter mein hum paanch algorithms padhenge: token bucket, leaking bucket, fixed window counter, sliding window log aur sliding window counter, aur phir Redis ke saath poora design banayenge.

A rate limiter controls how many requests a client or service may send in a given time. If someone goes over the limit, the extra requests are blocked (usually with a clear error message) until the time window allows more. You see rate limiters everywhere: a social app may allow only a few posts per hour, a signup page may allow a few account creations per day from one device, and a game may allow a reward to be claimed only a few times a week.

Why is this so useful? The notes list three main benefits. First, it prevents denial-of-service (DoS) attacks: when an attacker floods your API, a limiter stops the extra calls so the server does not run out of resources. Second, it reduces cost: fewer unnecessary requests means fewer servers needed, and it is especially important if you pay a third party for every call (for example a payment check or a credit check). Third, it prevents overload: it filters out excess traffic caused by bots or by clients with bugs, which keeps the servers stable for everyone else.

In this chapter we first agree on what we are building (a server-side API rate limiter), then decide where to place it, and then study five classic algorithms: token bucket, leaking bucket, fixed window counter, sliding window log and sliding window counter. At the end we put it together with Redis and talk about problems in distributed systems.

✨ Features

  • Limits how many requests a client can make in a time window.
  • Usually answers with HTTP 429 when the limit is passed.
  • Can be applied per user, per IP address, per API key or per endpoint.

✅ Benefits

  • Prevents DoS attacks by blocking excess calls and avoiding resource starvation.
  • Reduces cost by cutting unnecessary requests and server load.
  • Prevents overload by filtering excess traffic from bots or faulty clients.

⚠️ Problems

  • A badly chosen limit can block honest users.
  • It adds a little latency to every request.
  • In a distributed system it needs shared state and careful synchronization.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction + Benefits of Rate Limiting

This chapter explores the design and implementation of a rate limiter—a system component used to control traffic rates sent by clients or services. Rate limiters are crucial for preventing abuse, reducing costs, and ensuring the stability of server resources. Examples of their use include limiting posts, account creations, and reward claims.

  • Preventing DoS Attacks: Blocking excess calls to avoid resource starvation.
  • Cost Reduction: Limiting unnecessary requests to reduce server expenses.
  • Preventing Overloads: Filtering out excessive requests to stabilize server performance.

Interview questions and answers

What is a rate limiter?
A component that limits how many requests a client or service can send in a time period and rejects or delays the extra requests.
Why do we need a rate limiter?
To prevent DoS attacks, to reduce cost (especially with paid third-party APIs) and to prevent overload so the system stays stable.
Cross question: Is a rate limiter only a security tool?
No. It is also about fairness and cost control. It stops a single noisy client from using all the capacity, and it avoids paying for useless traffic.
What HTTP status code do you return?
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, often with headers that tell the client the limit, the remaining count and when to retry.

📝 Step 1: Understand the problem and the requirements

Hinglish samajh: Pehle hum features aur requirements tay karte hain. Features: server-side API rate limiter, kai throttle rules, distributed environment, alag service ya application code, aur throttle hone par user ko batana. Requirements: accurate throttling, kam latency, kam memory, distributed kaam karna, saaf exception handling aur high fault tolerance (limiter kharab ho to poora system na ruke). Isi se pata chalta hai ki counters memory mein aur shared store mein (jaise Redis) rakhne chahiye.

As the framework in chapter 3 says, we start by asking questions. The key features we agree on are these: it is a server-side API rate limiter; it must support multiple throttle rules (for example different limits for different endpoints or user types); it must work for a large-scale system in a distributed environment; it can be a separate service or code inside the application; and it should tell users when they are throttled.

The requirements are about quality. The limiter must be accurate: it should really block excess requests. It must have minimal latency, because it sits in front of every request and must not slow the HTTP response. It should use little memory. It must be distributed, so one limit can be shared across many servers or processes. It needs clear exception handling, so users see a helpful message when they are blocked. And it needs high fault tolerance: if the rate limiter has a problem, for example a cache server goes offline, the whole system must keep working.

These questions and requirements guide every choice that follows. For example, "minimal latency" and "low memory" tell us to prefer in-memory counters and simple algorithms, and "distributed" tells us that we need a shared store, not counters inside each web server.

Requirements and what they imply

RequirementWhat it meansDesign consequence
Accurate throttlingExcess requests are really blockedChoose the algorithm carefully
Low latencyMust not slow normal requestsKeep counters in memory
Low memoryLittle data per clientAvoid storing every request
DistributedOne limit across many serversUse a shared store such as Redis
Exception handlingUsers see a clear message when throttledReturn HTTP 429 with helpful headers
Fault toleranceA limiter failure must not take the system downFail open or use redundancy

✨ Features

  • Server-side limiting with many rules.
  • Works in a distributed environment.
  • Informs the user when throttled.

✅ Benefits

  • A clear target for the design.
  • Questions shrink the problem to a manageable size.
  • Requirements point directly to design choices.

⚠️ Problems

  • Tight accuracy and very low latency can pull in opposite directions.
  • Distributed accuracy is harder than single-server accuracy.
  • Deciding what to do when the limiter itself fails (allow or block) needs a business decision.

Interview questions and answers

What questions would you ask for a rate limiter design?
Is it client-side or server-side? What do we throttle by (IP, user, API key)? What is the scale? Is it a separate service or part of the code? Do users need to be informed when throttled?
What are the main requirements?
Accuracy, low latency, low memory use, distributed operation, clear exception handling and high fault tolerance.
Cross question: What should happen if the rate limiter fails?
Usually fail open (let requests through) so a limiter problem does not become an outage, unless blocking abuse is more important than availability for that API.
Why is low latency so important?
Because the limiter runs on every request. Any delay it adds is paid by all users.

📍 Step 2: Where should the rate limiter live?

Hinglish samajh: Rate limiter teen jagah rakha ja sakta hai: client side (bharosemand nahi kyunki requests nakli ho sakti hain), server side (aapke control mein) aur middleware jaise API gateway (sabse flexible). Middleware har request check karta hai aur ya to API servers ko bhejta hai ya seedha HTTP 429 deta hai. Chunav karte waqt apna tech stack dekho, sahi algorithm chuno, microservices hon to API gateway use karo, aur engineering resources kam hon to commercial gateway lo.

There are three places to put a rate limiter. The first is the client side. This is unreliable, because client requests can be forged by bad actors and you do not control what runs on someone else's device. So it cannot be your main defense.

The second is the server side: the limiter is part of your API servers. You control the code and you can trust it. The third is a middleware in front of the API servers, for example inside an API gateway. The middleware checks each request and either forwards it to the API servers or rejects it right away with HTTP 429. Cloud API gateways offer this as a managed feature, together with SSL termination, authentication and IP allow-listing.

How to choose? The notes give four guidelines. Look at your current technology stack (language, cache) and pick what runs efficiently there. Choose the algorithm that fits your business needs. If you already use microservices with an API gateway, add rate limiting there. If you do not have the engineering resources to build it, consider a commercial API gateway.

Comparing the options

PlacementControlReliabilityBest for
Client sideLow, anyone can bypass itUnreliableNever as the only protection
Server side (in the app)HighReliableRules that need business data
Middleware / API gatewayHigh and flexibleReliableMicroservices and shared rules

✨ Features

  • Three choices: client, server, middleware.
  • API gateways can provide rate limiting as a managed feature.
  • The choice depends on the stack, the algorithm and the resources you have.

✅ Benefits

  • Middleware keeps limiting logic in one place.
  • A gateway can protect many services at once.
  • Server-side control is trusted and flexible.

⚠️ Problems

  • Client-side limiting can be bypassed.
  • A gateway becomes a critical component and must be highly available.
  • Building your own limiter takes engineering time.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Step 2: High-Level Design

Placement Options

  1. Client-Side Implementation: Unreliable due to potential misuse.
  2. Server-Side Implementation: Preferred for control and reliability.
  3. Middleware (API Gateway): A flexible option for integrated rate limiting.

Guidelines for Placement

  • Evaluate current tech stack and choose efficient options.
  • Select appropriate algorithms based on business needs.
  • Use an API gateway if microservices are employed.
  • Opt for commercial solutions if resources are limited.

Interview questions and answers

Where would you put the rate limiter?
Server side, typically in a middleware such as an API gateway, because it is reliable and keeps the limiting logic out of each service.
Why is client-side limiting not enough?
Clients are not under your control and requests can be forged, so a malicious client can ignore the limit.
Cross question: Build or buy?
If you have a microservice architecture with a gateway, use its rate limiting. If you lack engineering resources, a commercial gateway can be quicker. Build your own when you need special rules.
What else can an API gateway do?
SSL termination, authentication, IP allow-listing, and serving static content, besides rate limiting.

🪣 Algorithm 1: Token bucket

Hinglish samajh: Token bucket mein ek bucket hota hai jisme tokens ek tay raftaar se daale jaate hain, jaise 4 token har minute. Har request ko ek token lena padta hai; token ho to request chali jaati hai, bucket khaali ho to request drop hoti hai. Do parameters hote hain: bucket ka size (kitna burst chalega) aur refill rate. Fayda: aasan, kam memory, aur chhote bursts allowed. Nuksan: dono parameters tune karna mushkil ho sakta hai aur kai buckets lag sakte hain.

The token bucket is the most popular algorithm and is used by big companies such as Amazon and Stripe. Imagine a bucket with a fixed capacity. A refiller drops tokens into the bucket at a steady rate, for example 4 tokens every minute. When the bucket is full, extra tokens are thrown away (they overflow). Every request must take one token. If a token is available, the request goes through. If the bucket is empty, the request is dropped.

There are two parameters: the bucket size (how many tokens it can hold, which is the largest burst allowed) and the refill rate (how many tokens are added per second, which is the long-term average rate). With a bucket size of 4 and a refill of 4 per minute, a user can send 4 requests at once, but then must wait for tokens to come back. Because the bucket stores unused tokens, a user who was quiet can send a short burst.

How many buckets do you need? It depends on the rules. Usually you need a different bucket for each API endpoint (for example one for creating posts, one for adding friends, one for liking posts). If you limit by IP address, you need one bucket per IP. If the whole system allows 10,000 requests per second, a single global bucket is enough.

How it works, step by step

  1. A refiller adds tokens to the bucket at a fixed rate.
  2. If the bucket is full, new tokens are discarded.
  3. A request arrives and tries to take one token.
  4. If a token exists, it is removed and the request is allowed.
  5. If the bucket is empty, the request is dropped.

A token bucket in C# (simple, single-process version)

public class TokenBucket
{
    private readonly int capacity;          ␀class="nu">0␀
    private readonly double refillPerSec;   ␀class="nu">1␀
    private double tokens;
    private DateTime last = DateTime.UtcNow;

    public TokenBucket(int capacity, double refillPerSec)
    {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerSec = refillPerSec;
        tokens = capacity;                  ␀class="nu">2␀
    }

    public bool TryTake()
    {
        lock (this)
        {
            var now = DateTime.UtcNow;
            ␀class="nu">3␀
            tokens = Math.Min(capacity, tokens + (now - last).TotalSeconds * refillPerSec);
            last = now;

            if (tokens >= class="nu">1) { tokens -= class="nu">1; return true; }   ␀class="nu">4␀
            return false;                                      ␀class="nu">5␀
        }
    }
}

✨ Features

  • Two parameters: bucket size and refill rate.
  • Allows short bursts up to the bucket size.
  • Widely used (for example by Amazon and Stripe).

✅ Benefits

  • Easy to implement.
  • Memory efficient: only a counter and a timestamp per bucket.
  • Supports bursts of traffic for a short time.

⚠️ Problems

  • The two parameters can be hard to tune.
  • You may need many buckets (per endpoint, per IP).
  • Allowing bursts is not always wanted.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 1. Token Bucket

  • Description: Tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token.
  • Parameters: Bucket size and refill rate.
  • Pros: Easy to implement, memory-efficient, supports traffic bursts.
  • Cons: Requires careful parameter tuning.

Interview questions and answers

How does the token bucket algorithm work?
A bucket holds tokens that are added at a fixed rate up to a maximum. Each request takes a token. If no token is available the request is rejected.
What are its parameters?
Bucket size (maximum burst) and refill rate (average allowed rate).
Cross question: How does it allow bursts?
If a client is idle, tokens pile up to the bucket size, so it can later send that many requests at once. After that, it is limited to the refill rate.
How many buckets do you need?
One per endpoint per client (for example per user or per IP) if you limit that way, or a single bucket if you only limit globally.
Cross question: How do you store the bucket in Redis?
Store the token count and the last refill time per key, and update them atomically (for example with a Lua script) so two requests cannot both take the last token.

🚰 Algorithm 2: Leaking bucket

Hinglish samajh: Leaking bucket ek queue ki tarah kaam karta hai. Request aati hai to queue mein jagah ho to jodi jaati hai, warna drop ho jaati hai. Queue se requests ek tay raftaar se nikalkar process hoti hain, jaise bucket ke chhote chhed se paani tapakta hai. Parameters: queue ka size aur outflow rate. Fayda: memory kam aur output stable. Nuksan: achanak burst aaye to purani requests queue bhar deti hain aur nayi requests late ya drop ho sakti hain.

The leaking bucket looks similar to the token bucket, but it works as a queue. When a request arrives, the system checks whether the queue is full. If there is space, the request is added to the end of the queue. If the queue is full, the request is dropped. Requests are then taken from the queue and processed at a fixed rate, like water dripping at a steady speed from a small hole in a bucket.

It has two parameters: the bucket (queue) size, which says how many requests can wait, and the outflow rate, which says how many requests are processed per second. The result is a very steady stream of requests to the backend, no matter how bursty the arrivals are. This is great when the backend needs a stable load, which is why it is used for things like shipping or payment processing queues. An open-source example is a Go rate-limit library from Uber.

The weakness is that a sudden burst fills the queue with old requests, so recent requests may have to wait or get dropped. The two parameters also need tuning. Compared with the token bucket, the leaking bucket protects the backend better, while the token bucket serves bursts better.

How it works, step by step

  1. A request arrives.
  2. If the queue has room, add the request to the end of the queue.
  3. If the queue is full, drop the request.
  4. At a fixed interval, take one request from the front and process it.

Token bucket vs leaking bucket

PointToken bucketLeaking bucket
IdeaRequests take tokensRequests wait in a queue
BurstsAllowed up to the bucket sizeAbsorbed by the queue, output stays steady
Output rateCan be burstyFixed
Extra requestsDropped when no tokensDropped when the queue is full
Good forAPIs that tolerate short burstsBackends that need smooth load

✨ Features

  • Uses a FIFO queue with a fixed size.
  • Processes requests at a fixed rate.
  • Parameters: bucket size and outflow rate.

✅ Benefits

  • Memory efficient because the queue size is limited.
  • Gives a stable, predictable outflow rate.
  • Good when the backend needs a smooth load.

⚠️ Problems

  • A burst of old requests can delay or starve recent requests.
  • Two parameters to tune.
  • Does not let a burst through quickly, even if the backend could handle it.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 2. Leaking Bucket

  • Description: Processes requests at a fixed rate using a FIFO queue.
  • Pros: Memory-efficient, stable outflow rate.
  • Cons: Traffic bursts may delay recent requests.

Example: https://github.com/uber-go/ratelimit

Interview questions and answers

How does a leaking bucket differ from a token bucket?
A leaking bucket is a queue processed at a fixed rate, so the output is smooth. A token bucket lets bursts through while tokens are available.
What are the parameters?
Bucket (queue) size and the outflow rate.
Cross question: When is the leaking bucket a bad choice?
When recent requests matter more than old ones, because a burst fills the queue with older requests and newer ones are delayed or dropped.
Where would you use it?
When the downstream system needs a constant load, for example a service that can only process a fixed number of jobs per second.

🪟 Algorithm 3: Fixed window counter

Hinglish samajh: Fixed window counter mein time ko fixed windows mein baanta jaata hai (jaise har minute) aur har window ka ek counter hota hai. Counter limit tak pahunch jaye to us window ki baaki requests drop ho jaati hain, aur nayi window par counter zero ho jaata hai. Ye bahut aasan aur kam memory wala hai. Samasya: window ke kinare par burst. Limit 5 per minute ho aur 2:00:30 se 2:01:00 tak 5 aur 2:01:00 se 2:01:30 tak 5 requests aayein to ek minute mein 10 requests nikal jaati hain, yaani limit se double.

The fixed window counter is the simplest idea. Divide time into fixed windows (for example every minute) and keep a counter for each window. Every request increases the counter by one. When the counter reaches the limit, all new requests in that window are dropped until the next window starts and the counter resets to zero.

For example, suppose the limit is 3 requests per second. In the first second, three requests are allowed and the fourth is dropped. When the next second begins, the counter is reset and requests are allowed again. It is very easy to implement and uses almost no memory: one counter per client per window. It also fits cases where quota should reset at fixed times, such as "100 calls per day".

The big problem is the edge of the window. Suppose the limit is 5 requests per minute and the windows are 2:00:00 to 2:01:00 and 2:01:00 to 2:02:00. A client sends 5 requests between 2:00:30 and 2:01:00 (allowed, window 1) and 5 more between 2:01:00 and 2:01:30 (allowed, window 2). In the one-minute period from 2:00:30 to 2:01:30 the server received 10 requests, twice the allowed quota. That is why fixed windows are not accurate when exact limits matter.

How it works, step by step

  1. Divide time into fixed windows (for example 1 minute).
  2. Keep a counter for each client and window.
  3. Increase the counter for each request.
  4. If the counter is above the limit, drop the request.
  5. When a new window starts, reset the counter.

Fixed window counter with Redis (INCR and EXPIRE)

␀class="nu">0␀
key = ␀class="nu">3␀ + floor(now / class="nu">60)

count = INCR key            ␀class="nu">1␀
if count == class="nu">1:
    EXPIRE key class="nu">60           ␀class="nu">2␀

if count > class="nu">100:
    reject with HTTP class="nu">429
else:
    allow

✨ Features

  • One counter per window.
  • Resets at fixed time boundaries.
  • Parameters: window length and request limit.

✅ Benefits

  • Very simple to implement and understand.
  • Memory efficient.
  • Fits quotas that reset at fixed times (for example per day).

⚠️ Problems

  • A burst at the window edge can allow up to twice the quota.
  • Not accurate for strict limits.
  • All clients reset at the same moment, which can cause a rush at the start of each window.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 3. Fixed Window Counter

  • Description: Divides time into fixed intervals and uses counters to limit requests.

Interview questions and answers

How does the fixed window counter work?
Time is cut into fixed windows. Each window has a counter. Requests increase it, and when it reaches the limit more requests are dropped until the next window.
What is its main problem?
Traffic that arrives at the end of one window and the start of the next can exceed the limit, up to twice the quota in a short period.
Cross question: Give a concrete example of the edge problem.
With a limit of 5 per minute, 5 requests at 2:00:30 to 2:01:00 and 5 more at 2:01:00 to 2:01:30 all pass, so 10 requests arrive within one minute.
When is it still a good choice?
When you need a simple quota that resets at fixed times and slight inaccuracy at the edges is acceptable.

📜 Algorithm 4: Sliding window log

Hinglish samajh: Sliding window log har request ka timestamp yaad rakhta hai (jaise Redis sorted set mein). Nayi request aane par window se purane timestamps hata deta hai, naya timestamp jodta hai, aur agar log ka size limit ke andar hai to request allow karta hai warna reject. Isme edge burst wali samasya nahi hoti, isliye ye bahut accurate hai. Par har request ka timestamp store hone se memory zyada lagti hai.

The sliding window log fixes the edge problem of the fixed window by remembering exactly when each request happened. It keeps a log of timestamps, usually in a cache such as a Redis sorted set. When a new request arrives, the algorithm first removes all timestamps that are older than the start of the current window (that is, older than "now minus window length"). Then it adds the new request's timestamp to the log. If the log size is within the allowed count, the request is accepted; otherwise it is rejected.

Here is an example with a limit of 2 requests per minute. A request arrives at 1:00:01 and the log is empty, so it is added and allowed. Another arrives at 1:00:30; the log has 2 entries, so it is allowed. A request at 1:00:50 makes the log size 3, which is above the limit, so it is rejected (its timestamp may still stay in the log). A new request arrives at 1:01:40. Entries before 1:00:40 (one minute ago) are removed, which removes the first two, and the log then holds only 1:00:50 and 1:01:40: size 2, so the request is allowed.

Because the window truly slides with each request, this method is very accurate: in any rolling window the number of allowed requests never exceeds the limit. The cost is memory. Even rejected requests may be stored, so the log can be large when the limit is high or the traffic is heavy.

How it works, step by step

  1. Keep a log of timestamps for each client.
  2. When a request arrives, remove timestamps older than the window.
  3. Add the new timestamp to the log.
  4. If the log size is within the limit, allow the request.
  5. Otherwise reject it.

Sliding window log with a Redis sorted set

␀class="nu">0␀
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rate:user42 class="nu">0 (now_ms - class="nu">60000)   ␀class="nu">1␀
ZADD rate:user42 now_ms now_ms                      ␀class="nu">2␀
EXPIRE rate:user42 class="nu">60                               ␀class="nu">3␀
size = ZCARD rate:user42                            ␀class="nu">4␀

if size > class="nu">100: reject (HTTP class="nu">429) else: allow
␀class="nu">5␀

✨ Features

  • Keeps timestamps in a sorted structure.
  • Removes entries older than the window on each request.
  • Parameters: window length and request limit.

✅ Benefits

  • Very accurate: no edge bursts.
  • Works in any rolling window.
  • Straightforward to reason about.

⚠️ Problems

  • High memory use: it stores a timestamp for every request (even rejected ones).
  • Cleaning and counting the log costs CPU for large logs.
  • Hard to afford for very high limits.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 4. Sliding Window Log

  • Description: Tracks timestamps to allow a rolling time window.
  • Pros: Accurate rate limiting.

Interview questions and answers

How does the sliding window log work?
It stores the timestamp of each request, removes timestamps older than the window when a new request arrives, and allows the request if the number of remaining timestamps is within the limit.
Why is it more accurate than the fixed window?
Because it looks at the true last N seconds for every request, not at fixed calendar windows, so edge bursts cannot sneak through.
Cross question: What is its main weakness?
Memory. It stores one entry per request, so heavy traffic and high limits make the logs big.
Which Redis structure suits it?
A sorted set, with the timestamp as the score, so that old entries can be removed by score and the size counted quickly.

🧮 Algorithm 5: Sliding window counter

Hinglish samajh: Sliding window counter fixed window aur sliding log ka mel hai. Ye sirf do counters rakhta hai (abhi wali window aur pichhli window) aur rolling window ka anumaan lagata hai: abhi ka count + pichhla count x overlap ka hissa. Example: limit 7 per minute, pichhle minute mein 5, abhi tak 3, aur nayi request minute ke 30% par aayi: 3 + 5 x 0.7 = 6.5, round down 6, jo 7 se kam hai, isliye allow. Memory kam lagti hai aur spikes smooth hote hain, par ye ek approximation hai.

The sliding window counter is a hybrid. It combines the low memory of the fixed window counter with the smoothness of the sliding log. It keeps counters for fixed windows only (the current one and the previous one), and then estimates how many requests happened in the rolling window using a weighted sum.

The common formula is: requests in the rolling window = requests in the current window + requests in the previous window x overlap percentage, where the overlap percentage is how much of the rolling window still falls inside the previous window. Example: the limit is 7 requests per minute. The previous minute had 5 requests, the current minute has 3 so far, and a new request arrives 30% of the way into the current minute. The rolling window covers the last 70% of the previous minute, so the estimate is 3 + 5 x 0.7 = 6.5, which is rounded down to 6. Since 6 is below 7, the request is allowed.

This is a good compromise. It is memory efficient (just two counters per client), it smooths out spikes because the rate is based on the average of the previous window, and it handles bursts well. The downside is that it is an approximation: it assumes the requests in the previous window were spread evenly. Experiments reported by large providers show that the error is very small in practice, so it works well for most real systems.

How it works, step by step

  1. Keep counters for the current and the previous fixed window.
  2. Work out how much of the previous window still overlaps the rolling window.
  3. Estimate = current count + previous count x overlap.
  4. Allow the request if the estimate is below the limit.
  5. Rotate the counters when a new window starts.

The estimate in code (C#)

␀class="nu">0␀
bool Allow(int currentCount, int previousCount, double secondsIntoWindow, int windowSeconds, int limit)
{
    double overlap = (windowSeconds - secondsIntoWindow) / windowSeconds; ␀class="nu">1␀
    double estimate = currentCount + previousCount * overlap;
    return Math.Floor(estimate) < limit;      ␀class="nu">2␀
}

✨ Features

  • Only two counters per client.
  • Weighted sum of the previous and current window.
  • Parameters: window length and request limit.

✅ Benefits

  • Memory efficient.
  • Smooths out spikes in traffic.
  • No sharp edge bursts like the fixed window.

⚠️ Problems

  • It is an approximation, not an exact count.
  • It assumes that requests in the previous window were evenly spread.
  • Slightly more complex than the fixed window counter.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 5. Sliding Window Counter

  • Description: Combines fixed window and sliding log methods for smoothing spikes.
  • Pros: Memory-efficient, handles traffic bursts.
  • Cons: Approximation may not be perfectly strict.

Interview questions and answers

How does the sliding window counter work?
It keeps counters for the current and previous fixed windows and estimates the rolling window as current count plus previous count times the overlap fraction.
Work out an example.
Limit 7 per minute, previous window 5, current window 3, request 30% into the current minute: 3 + 5 x 0.7 = 6.5, round down to 6, which is below 7, so allow.
Cross question: Why choose it over the sliding log?
It needs far less memory (two numbers instead of a log of timestamps) and gives a very close answer, which is good enough for most services.
What is its drawback?
It is not exact, because it assumes the previous window's requests were uniformly distributed.

🏗️ High-level architecture with Redis

Hinglish samajh: Rate limiter ka basic idea counter hai: is client ne kitni requests bheji hain aur kya limit paar hui? Counters tez aur sabhi servers ke liye shared hone chahiye, isliye Redis jaisa in-memory cache use hota hai (INCR counter badhata hai aur EXPIRE usse tay samay baad hata deta hai). Flow: client middleware ko request bhejta hai, middleware Redis se counter padhta hai, limit hui to HTTP 429, nahi to counter badhakar request API servers ko bhejta hai. Rules disk par rakhe jaate hain aur cache kiye jaate hain.

The basic idea of any rate limiter is a counter: how many requests has this client sent, and is it over the limit? The counters must be fast and shared between servers, so a database on disk is too slow. The notes suggest an in-memory cache such as Redis. Redis is a good fit because it is very fast, supports a time-based expiry on keys, and offers handy commands: INCR adds 1 to a counter and EXPIRE removes it after a set time.

The flow is simple. First, the client sends a request to the rate limiter middleware. Second, the middleware fetches the counter for the right bucket or window from Redis and checks whether the limit is reached. Third, if the limit is reached, the request is rejected; if not, the request goes on to the API servers, and the counter is increased and saved back to Redis.

A more complete design adds a few more parts. The rules (for example "max 5 marketing messages per day") are stored on disk in configuration files and loaded into a cache, so workers can read them quickly. When a request is rejected, the limiter returns HTTP 429 and may add headers: how many calls are allowed in the window, how many remain, and how many seconds to wait. Rejected requests can be dropped or sent to a queue to be processed later (this is called a throttled request).

How it works, step by step

  1. The client sends a request to the rate limiter middleware.
  2. The middleware loads the rule and fetches the counter from Redis.
  3. If the limit is reached, it returns HTTP 429 (or queues the request).
  4. If not, it increases the counter, saves it, and forwards the request.
  5. Response headers tell the client the limit, the remaining count and when to retry.

Useful response headers (common practice)

HeaderMeaning
X-Ratelimit-LimitHow many calls are allowed per window
X-Ratelimit-RemainingHow many calls are left in the window
X-Ratelimit-Retry-AfterSeconds to wait before trying again

✨ Features

  • Counters live in Redis with an expiry.
  • Rules come from configuration and are cached.
  • Rejected requests get HTTP 429 and helpful headers.

✅ Benefits

  • Redis makes counter operations fast.
  • Counters are shared by all servers.
  • Rules can change without redeploying the code.

⚠️ Problems

  • Redis becomes a critical dependency: it needs replication and failover.
  • Every request adds a network call to Redis.
  • Counter updates must be atomic (see the next lesson).

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · High-Level Architecture

  • Data Storage: Use in-memory caching (e.g., Redis) for fast counter operations.
  • Steps:
    1. Client sends request to middleware.
    2. Middleware checks counters in Redis.
    3. Request is processed or rejected based on limits.

Interview questions and answers

Where do you store the counters and why?
In an in-memory store like Redis, because it is fast, shared by all servers, and supports key expiry so old counters disappear automatically.
Describe the request flow.
Client to the rate limiter middleware, which reads the counter and rules, then either rejects (429) or increments the counter and forwards the request to the API servers.
Cross question: What happens to throttled requests?
They can be dropped with an HTTP 429, or in some systems put in a queue to be processed later.
How does the client know when to retry?
Through response headers such as the remaining quota and a retry-after value.

🌐 Distributed rate limiting, performance and monitoring

Hinglish samajh: Distributed system mein do badi dikkatein hain: race condition (do requests ek hi counter padhkar dono pass ho jaati hain aur limit paar ho jaati hai) aur synchronization (alag alag limiter servers ke counters alag ho jaate hain). Race condition ka hal hai Lua script ya Redis ke atomic commands. Synchronization ka hal hai centralized store jaise Redis. Performance ke liye multiple data centers aur eventual consistency use karte hain. Monitoring se dekhte hain ki algorithm aur rules sahi kaam kar rahe hain ya nahi.

Building a limiter for one server is easy. Building it for many servers and many data centers is where the real challenges appear. The notes name two main ones: race conditions and synchronization.

A race condition happens when two requests read the same counter at the same moment. Suppose the counter is 3 and the limit is 4. Both requests read "3", both decide they are allowed and both write "4". The real count should be 5, so the limit is exceeded. Locks would fix this but they slow the system down. Better solutions are a Lua script in Redis (the whole check-and-update runs as one atomic step) or Redis sorted sets with atomic commands.

The synchronization issue appears with many rate limiter servers. If client 1 sends a request to limiter A and the next to limiter B, and each keeps its own counter, neither knows about the other. One option is sticky sessions (always send a client to the same limiter), but this is not scalable or flexible. A better solution is a centralized data store, such as Redis, that all the limiters share.

For performance, use several data centers (edge locations) so that users hit a nearby limiter, and use an eventual consistency model to synchronize data between locations instead of waiting for every update to spread. For monitoring, collect analytics to check two things: is the algorithm effective, and are the rules working? If the rules are too strict, honest requests are dropped, so loosen them. If there is a sudden traffic spike (for example a flash sale), you may need a different algorithm such as token bucket, which handles bursts.

Problems and solutions

ProblemWhat goes wrongSolution
Race conditionTwo requests read the same count and both passLua scripts or atomic Redis commands (sorted sets)
SynchronizationEach limiter keeps its own counterA centralized shared store such as Redis
Latency for far usersDistant users wait for a central limiterMulti-data center or edge deployment
Cross-location syncUpdating all locations immediately is slowEventual consistency between locations
Wrong rulesToo strict blocks honest users, too loose lets abuse inMonitor analytics and adjust

Atomic fixed-window check in Redis with Lua

␀class="nu">0␀
local count = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[class="nu">1])
if count == class="nu">1 then
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[class="nu">1], ARGV[class="nu">2])
end
if count > tonumber(ARGV[class="nu">1]) then
  return class="nu">0      ␀class="nu">1␀
end
return class="nu">1        ␀class="nu">2␀
␀class="nu">3␀

✨ Features

  • Atomic operations remove race conditions.
  • A shared store synchronizes many limiters.
  • Multi-data center setups reduce latency.

✅ Benefits

  • The limit is enforced correctly across the whole system.
  • Users get quick responses from nearby locations.
  • Analytics show whether the rules fit the real traffic.

⚠️ Problems

  • Locks are accurate but slow.
  • Eventual consistency can briefly allow slightly more than the limit.
  • The shared store must be highly available.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Advanced Considerations

Distributed Environments

  • Challenges: Race conditions, synchronization issues.
  • Solutions: Use locks, Lua scripts, or sorted sets in Redis. Employ centralized data stores for synchronization.

Performance Optimizations

  • Multi-data center setups for reduced latency.
  • Eventual consistency models for synchronization.

Monitoring

  • Regular analytics to ensure algorithm effectiveness and adjust rules as needed.

Interview questions and answers

What is a race condition in a rate limiter?
Two concurrent requests read the same counter value, both decide to allow, and both write back the same new value, so one increment is lost and the limit can be exceeded.
How do you fix it?
Make the check-and-update atomic, for example with a Redis Lua script or with sorted-set commands. Locks also work but are slower.
Cross question: How do multiple limiter servers share limits?
They store the counters in a centralized data store such as Redis rather than in local memory, so every server sees the same numbers.
What would you monitor?
Whether the algorithm works for the traffic pattern, whether the rules block too many legitimate users, how often requests are throttled, and Redis latency and availability.
Cross question: What if Redis fails?
Decide a policy in advance: usually fail open (allow requests) so the service stays available, while alerting the team. Use Redis replication and failover to make this rare.

⚖️ Choosing an algorithm: comparison and summary

Hinglish samajh: Paanch algorithms ka saar: burst allow karna ho aur memory kam ho to token bucket; backend ko steady load chahiye to leaking bucket; sabse aasan chahiye aur edge burst chalega to fixed window counter; poori accuracy chahiye aur memory de sakte ho to sliding window log; smooth aur kam memory wala chahiye to sliding window counter. Interview mein pehle puchho ki sabse zaroori kya hai, phir ek chuno aur uska trade-off batao.

You now know five algorithms. The best one depends on what your system needs most, and you should be able to defend your choice in an interview. This lesson compares them side by side. (The comparison table is my summary of the notes above.)

If you need to allow short bursts and want a simple, memory-light solution, choose the token bucket. If the backend needs a perfectly steady load, choose the leaking bucket. If you want the simplest thing and can accept edge-of-window bursts, choose the fixed window counter. If you need strict accuracy and can pay for the memory, choose the sliding window log. If you want a smooth, accurate-enough limit with low memory, choose the sliding window counter.

In an interview, start by asking what matters (bursts, accuracy, memory, steady output), then choose one and mention the trade-off. You can say: "I would start with a token bucket in Redis behind the API gateway, because it handles bursts and uses little memory. If we need stricter accuracy, I would consider a sliding window counter."

Five algorithms at a glance

AlgorithmMemoryHandles burstsAccuracyMain weakness
Token bucketLowYes, up to the bucket sizeGoodTwo parameters to tune
Leaking bucketLow (fixed queue)Smooths them into a steady rateGoodRecent requests can be delayed by old ones
Fixed window counterVery lowPoorly at window edgesLow at edgesUp to twice the quota at window boundaries
Sliding window logHighYesVery highStores every timestamp
Sliding window counterLowYesGood (approximate)Assumes even spread in the previous window

✨ Features

  • Five algorithms with different trade-offs.
  • Token bucket and sliding window counter are the most common choices.
  • The choice depends on bursts, accuracy and memory.

✅ Benefits

  • A clear decision path for interviews.
  • You can explain why you rejected the alternatives.
  • The same table helps in real projects.

⚠️ Problems

  • No algorithm is best at everything.
  • Real traffic may need different algorithms for different APIs.
  • The table gives guidance, not exact numbers.

Interview questions and answers

Which algorithm would you choose and why?
Usually a token bucket (bursts allowed, simple, low memory) or a sliding window counter (smooth, low memory, good accuracy), depending on whether bursts are welcome. I would explain the trade-off.
Compare fixed window and sliding window log.
Fixed window is simple and cheap but can allow double the quota at window edges. Sliding log is exact but stores every timestamp, so it uses a lot of memory.
Cross question: Can you use different algorithms in one system?
Yes. For example a token bucket for public API calls and a fixed window for a daily quota, each chosen for what that rule needs.
Cross question: How would you design the rate limiter in 45 minutes?
Clarify requirements, place the limiter in a gateway, choose an algorithm and justify it, add Redis for shared counters, and discuss race conditions, multi-region deployment and monitoring.
